column2: 86,525,000 principal amount with interest since June 30, 1931.
Indebtedness incurred in 1919; funded in 1923.

No payment on account of principal or interest has been received since the payment due June 30, 1931. Payments due in the year 1931-32, totalling $563,250, were deferred in accordance with the international moratorium on inter-governmental debts. Subsequently Greece deferred payment on its external indebtedness, whether held by governments or the public.

hon. Secretary of State. There is a clause in the amended Ontario Electoral Act which I believe interferes with federal rights. 1038252,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.4.3,1934-06-11,b2723513-c609-4a5c-87f4-bd7c225ccd75,ca.m.2309,Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):,Minister of Trade and Commerce,EXPORT PRICE OF NICKEL,,,Mr. Speaker, the question

asked by the hon. gentleman is a very difficult one to discuss or answer in the way which he has in mind. The bureau of statistics, under the Statistics Act, a statute of this country which definitely and absolutely controls its activities, secures information from various sources which is strictly confidential. It is provided by that act-I think the same thing applies to other information under other statutes-that where the information is from one firm and the publication of that information would be a disclosure of the firm's private affairs, it is not competent for an official to give out the information. As far as he has been able to do so the dominion statistician has complied with the request. Personally, I think it is unfair to discuss the affairs of an industry which is in fact a single company industry under, shall I say-I do not blame my hon. friend in this respect-the guise of public statistics. I am sorry it has not been possible to give publicly the answer which the hon. gentleman desires but I think he will agree that I have done everything which could be reasonably expected to be done to meet his wishes. I should be very glad to discuss this further with him but the fact remains that there is a statute which controls the officials of the government. If the hon. gentleman would intimate to me privately any further information he desires, I will have an investigation made within the ambit of the statute and see if we cannot meet his wishes.

1038269,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.8.2,1934-06-11,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. NEILL:,,SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT,,,"I wonder if the minister would give us some information in regard to this matter. There does not seem to be a section with respect to the title on which we could discuss the general principles of the bill, but perhaps he will allow me to ask him some questions under this section. In moving the
Soldier Settlement Act

first reading of the bill the minister indicated that it was to be done at the request of various municipalities-rural municipalities-and inferentially we gathered that it was going to help the settler. I would ask him however wherein this act would do the one or the other. The municipality is not going to be put in the position, as we thought it was, of getting taxes from the government, but merely the land, which it does not want. Possibly the minister will reassure us by intimating that it is the intention of the government to pay the taxes, although it does not state so 'here.

The other point on which I should like some information is this. Under the third section, on the municipality instituting proceedings, which is rather an indefinite way of expressing it, the settler's contract of sale with the soldier settlement board is automatically rescinded. Is not that going to work a serious hardship on the soldier settler? The government have the right to-day to rescind the agreement upon non-payment; but they have recognized from time to time, and quite properly, that when times are very bad and farmers who own their land, free of any debt or mortgage, cannot make a living on it, then the settler certainly cannot make annual payments, and the government have made reasonable allowance in cases of that kind. I think hon. members can be assured that in administering this law no municipality will pick out a soldier settler and impose upon him something which is not imposed generally upon all settlers. If what some hon. members have suggested is true, that no settler can pay anything, I do not think it will make much difference to the municipality, the settler or anybody else. However, in the light of the facts which discloses that the soldier settler ag a class is probably the best taxpayer, I do not entertain those views. As I have said, there are municipalities which have had very severe burdens placed upon their treasuries because of the withdrawal of lands for tax purposes. Roads have been extended, school-houses built and services rendered by municipalities which in a large measure have been built up by reason of these municipalities. I think the municipality should have the rigjit of recourse to lands held by the director. The municipality is in a better position to determine whether or not proceedings by way of tax sale should be enforced strictly, particularly when the director still reserves to himself the right which he has always had when a settler does not redeem. Under the provincial statutes he may step in and redeem the land and, if it is a proper case, make a new agreement with the settler. The essence of this legislation is an endeavour on the part of the government to relieve the municipalities of the situation which I have indicated and to make the lands held by the director as a corporation available to be placed on the assessment rolls of the municipalities and be subject to taxation, whether or not there is a soldier settler upon them. I do not think hon. members need have much fear that a settler who is trying to pay for his land will find himself in a less favourable position than he is to-day. Under the legislation of last year a large number of soldier settlers paid their taxes and have become entitled to the bonus provided by that legislation-

What I want to open up at this time is perhaps a larger question. At that gathering in Saskatoon it would appear that a rather different and new line of policy was taken. It was worked out on the understanding that a policy of accord could be satisfactorily adhered to by both parties, that is the soldier settlers and the department, if certain legislation were brought down. That legislation was brought down last year; it was put through the house and it has been in existence during the past year. Apparently from the reports I have at hand the good effects of that legislation are somewhat in danger. Seemingly the collection policy of the department is under serious consideration by the settlers and it should receive some discussion in the house. The minister and the department will no doubt take the stand that they are doing their best to collect the money for the state and that is always a duty with regard to those who are collecting taxes from men who are in the position in which we find the soldier settlers. But some of the soldier settlers on the other hand take the stand that the policy is ruthless, harsh and that if it is persisted in they will lose their farms and will be driven off the land. To put the matter in a nutshell, may I read a letter addressed to me by H. S. Packman, general secretary of the Soldier Settlers' Union, dated at Lloydminster, February 4, 1934. This opens up practically the whole question of policy between the soldier settlers throughout the dominion and the department. The letter reads as follows:
Whereas, we, the delegates-
It is really a resolution.

-representing the locals of the Soldier Settlers' Union, present at the convention held at Lloydminster, Saskatchewan, October 25 and 26, 1933, have decided that, we have not and are not, deviating in any way from our main objective, and that, we were quite willing to accept the temporary legislation for the period stated providing, the promise made by the director of soldier settlement at the Saskatoon conference in 1933, concerning the collection policy of the department was kept.

It is regretted that in many instances this promise lias been violated, and therefore we feel that we are not held to our promise given, to refrain from asking the government for any further concessions during the period of the temporary legislation.
That is, during the next three or four years.
Therefore, be it resolved that:-

We, the soldier settlers, in conference do not consider the recent legislation passed by parliament as being the solution to our permanent establishment, and we consider that the following will prove to be more effective.
Then follows the climax of their resolution:
That our total debt to date be as it stood at the completion of the 30 per cent reduction in 1930 and henceforth be a non-interest bearing debt.

That opens up, as I said, the question of the collection policy of the government and I shall cite some instances showing rather harsh collection methods. Before I put one or two of them on record and ask the minister about them, perhaps he might have something to say in reply to this resolution from the Soldier Settlers' Union, the headquarters of Which is at Lloydminster, Saskatchewan. Permit me to explain.

On the morning of Thanksgiving Day, fall 1933, careless shooters from Saskatoon destroyed my entire crop by fire (presumed to be wads from low grade shells in the stacks) then in bin, with threshing just completed. Bin stood between two stacks of straw -one oat, the other wheat, as the bin had been divided and oats threshed in one end and wheat in the other. The matter was reported to mounted police, who investigated, and also to S.S.B. and the Star, who reported upon it. However, no one was apprehended, and' the loss was most complete, so much so that I was unable to meet my threshing expenses, and the winter has been the most hard I have ever experienced.

This bin was built by me in 1922. from my own funds and to receive the crop from a 100 acre parcel of land in which T was then interested to the east, and skidded on 6"" x 6"" skids-its cost being around $150. Releasing this 100 acre parcel around 1926, the bin was then hauled home for general use, and has since received crops from other fields.

It carried an insurance of $75. covered by joint policy in favour of S.S.B. and self, and in signing proof of loss I was able to get the full amount on account of the good construction of the bin-signing an agreement for company to draft cheque in name of S.S.B. believing I could immediately get a reimbursement and reconstruct the bin.
Now comes the climax of his letter:

Everything was explained to the superintendent of the S.S.B.-loss of all fodder and straw, bin, and all grain that might be used for seed or other than pig feed, and that I had no cover for this grain as this was my only bin for grain storage, and the grain lay in the open. He replied he would take it up at once with headquarters, but two months elapsed before he replied to me and then by reason of pressure brought to bear by letter from myself. I enclose this final letter. -

Its contents are self explanatory. They are retaining the $75 on the grounds that because of my account they cannot reimburse me. No mention of the legal rights of the case or to whom this $75 really belongs, and I am assured that it is mine by two lawyers in Saskatoon.
How do I stand upon this matter, and can the union give me any help.
He was writing the Soldier Settlers' Union.
Personally I doubt the statement that this is a ruling of headquarters unless the new director at headquarters is oversharp.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,George Gibson Coote,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038424,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.38,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,Without entering into a long discussion as to the circumstances which must combine to bring about the adjudication that any person is bankrupt, I can only say that an insolvent man is one who is unable to meet his debts as they mature. That is the general broad definition of the term. The Bankruptcy Act provides that under certain contingencies where a person is not able to meet his obligations as they mature, application may be made to have him adjudged a bankrupt. When he is so adjudged certain results follow which are provided for by the statute. That does not apply to a farmer exce'pt in a limited way, as will be seen in the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act itself. What is proposed now is the adoption of the general principle of the Bankruptcy Act. A farmer who is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due may make a proposal for a composition, an extension of time or a scheme or arrangement, either before or after assignment has been made. That is a
column2: voluntary

column1: from a compulsory assignment. If I am unable to meet my obligations and a petition is filed that I be adjudged a bankrupt, that would be one class of assignment. The second class is where I. realizing that fact, may be an assignment. There are innumerable cases such as this and we see them in the Gazette every week. A man ""assigns for the benefit of his creditors"" was the term used before we had the Bankruptcy Act, that was the term used in the provisions of the statute relating to assignments for the benefit of creditors. That assignment act had its origin in the legislature of Ontario and was held by the courts to be valid until such time as this parliament determined that it would exercise its jurisdiction over the whole country. Since the passing of the Bankruptcy Act it is no longer an assignment for the benefit of creditors, it is an assignment in bankruptcy.

The statute itself provides for the method by which property is to be distributed among the creditors, their order of priority and matters of that kind. This proposal is to take care of the farmer who is not in a position to meet his obligations. Instead of assigning or taking the benefits of the Bankruptcy Act, if its provisions were extended to him, he suggests to his creditors that if he is given an extension of time he may be able to work out his liabilities.

1038496,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.110,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,I am sure the hon. members for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) and Melville (Mr. Motherwell) will understand me when I say that part of this is somewhat intricate and technical, all bankruptcy laws have been found so to be. He has a mortgage against his property. He has suffered crop failures, but now he begins to see some signs of returning prosperity; there is more moisture in the ground, and so on. He says, "" If I had a chance I could pay my creditors, either in full or at least in a certain proportion. I do not desire to have my property cleaned up and sold; I desire to stay here with my implements and my accumulations and work my property. I ask the law to restrain my creditors from coming in and closing me out with an execution in the courts of the province,"" because this overcomes that difficulty as well. ""I ask that to be stopped, and I say I should be given a chance."" There-

upon the official receiver under this act discusses his problem with him. The creditors are called together, and the farmer says, "" I am not trying to get out of paying my debts; I want to pay them if you will give me time in which to do it."" We have taken steps to protect him up to that point, and that agreement is confirmed. But supposing there are some creditors who say no. 1038500,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.114,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,Quite so, in the absence of a statute. If I might make it clear, there is what might be called the written law and the unwritten law. The unwritten law, the common law, provides that a settlement between creditors and debtors cannot be made unless all the creditors agree, for my debt cannot be disposed of by anyone else in the world but myself. That is a striking tribute to that individuality of purpose which has been referred to in this house from time to time. In the early days in Great Britain, as in other countries, it was found that it was desirable for the honest man-and I use that term very emphatically-to be able to get a fresh start by making a full disclosure o,f everything he owned and handing it over to a trustee, who was usual!}' a statutory trustee, who sold it, took out his expenses and distributed the proceeds rateably among the creditors. But that did not make him a free man; he then had to make application to the judge in bankruptcy for the purpose of receiving his discharge. In England to-day, if you are interested and will pick up the newspapers day after day. you will find that applications are

made for discharge which are opposed on the ground that the man had not given all his property to the trustee, that he had gone on and earned money after making the assignment which had not been made available for his creditors. So there he is, faced with the certainty that he cannot sit in parliament if he is an adjudicated bankrupt, and that he may not hold manj' offices that are mentioned in statutes and that have grown up under common law. He is still branded as an undischarged bankrupt.

This act seeks to secure for the farmer the benefits of that principle, set up by machinery that will run easily and without expense to the farmer. But if he makes what I might call a too optimistic adjustment and fails to carry it out then, under this statute, he becomes liable to be adjudicated a bankrupt, because that is to constitute an act of bankruptcy. On the other hand I think I shall adopt the suggestion that has been made and add the words, ""if the judge or a court so determine."" In other words it does not follow automatically, which is the fear of the hon. member. There may be, and I think there is, something in that. On the other hand if the farmer makes his composition and meets it, when the composition is met his creditors are paid, either at fifty or sixty cents on the dollar or, over a long period of time, one hundred cents on the dollar or whatever it may be. That is a matter in which the voice of the creditors is not going to be final under this statute. This is the difficulty that any legal gentleman in the house will agree we have had to meet, and if I do say it myself- authors are always proud of their products-I think it has been not unfairly met by this legislation. We have provided that the farmers are to get a chance to stay on their land, utilizing the assets they have and working out their destinies, paying their debts not necessarily at one hundred cents on the dollar but to the extent which may be agreed upon between the creditors and the debtor or, failing that, by the action of the review board for the province.

There are those two classes, and one is quite distinct from the other.

With regard to the down-and-outer, I was appealing to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) if there was not some way of letting that man feel that he was free, free without any strings whatsoever, because after all these matters are to be determined by a judge and the law can be administered in a strange way sometimes. I have great faith in the judiciary of Canada, yet nevertheless there is the humane judge who will administer the law humanly, and there is the other judge who takes the attitude:

I would appeal to the Prime Minister to use his great talents to devise some scheme that will permit the applicant who is honestly eligible to complete discharge from all his present mortgage obligations, who has not played the part of either an Ananias or a Sapphira, who has not been making wrong returns-I have no use for him, but there have been at least the two before-mentioned historic examples and there have been others since-to have a chance to start over again as free men and women. I am speaking for the man who has made his returns properly, who has not been trying to humbug anybody, who has not been trying to put something over the government or anybody else, that he be given the opportunity to start over again feeling that if he complies with the conditions he can go free.

Let me illustrate. When Abraham Lincoln set the slaves of the south free, I do not know how many strings were on those slaves, but there were some strings, I recall about runaway slaves and all that sort of thing. Speaking generally, however, those slaves were set free although sometimes they had become so much attached to their masters that they did not want to leave. Now if the right hon. leader of the government could meet the situation I have spoken of in some way, and I think it could be done, he would be looked upon as the great emancipator of the white slaves of

Canada-I am speaking very seriously, Mr Chairman-just as Abraham Lincoln was the emancipator of the dark slaves of the south. Why not put in a proviso that the law shall be administered thus and so, and with the understanding that it is the government's desire to free all men who are honestly worthy of being made free? That khould not be impossible. I think I could make a stab at something like that myself in the way of rough draftsmanship, and I am confident that the Prime Minister, who I feel sure understands me, could draft something to meet that situation. Look at another incidental advantage such a policy would be, Mr. Chairman. Most of the people in this house are capitalists; that is, they believe in the capitalist system as such, even though imperfect. All farmers are capitalists. What is the use of talking nonsense about socialism or communism as long as we own land? Now if the Prime Minister would do as I suggest, look what a tribute it would be to a reformed capitalism, harnessed up, if you like, adjusted to suit the requirements of to-day. It would stop the mouths of these men who are talking socialism and nihilism and communism and all these other isms, and decrying the capitalist system because it is defective. Of course, it is defective.

column1: institutions will be defective as long as we as individuals who comprise the community are defective ourselves. But I do not think we have the power to do what the hon. gentleman suggests, and I think perhaps on reconsideration he would doubt the wisdom of it himself.

The discussion so far has raised several questions, and I think we have disposed of most of them except that which arises under subsection 3 of section 2. The section as it reads places upon the farmer as a punishment for default the possibility of an application being made to have him adjudicated a bankrupt, it being declared to be an act of insolvency. The hon. member for Melville asked a very proper question as to what constitutes an act of insolvency. That is covered by section 3 of the Bankruptcy Act, and without reading it at length-perhaps the hon. gentleman will excuse me from reading too much-I shall just give the purport of it as I proceed.
First of all, if in Canada or elsewhere a debtor makes an assignment of his property

to a trustee for the benefit of his creditors generally, whether it is an assignment authorized by the Bankruptcy Act or not, that constitutes an act of insolvency. Or if he makes a fraudulent conveyance, gift, delivery, or transfer of his property, the words ""fraudulent conveyance"" having a meaning attributed to them by the courts, that is an act of insolvency. Or if he makes a conveyance or transfer of his property which in itself would be void as a fraudulent preference if he were adjudged bankrupt-that is a technical matter -that is an act of insolvency. Or if he endeavours to defeat or delay his creditors, that also is an act of insolvency.

Next is the one which is the most common. Or if h'e permits any execution or other process issued against him under which any of his goods are seized, levied upon or taken in execution to remain unsatisfied until within four days from the time fixed by the sheriff for the sale thereof, and so on, that is the customary and ordinary case in which bankruptcy is determined, or at least I put it that way. The next paragraph reads:

If he exhibits to any meeting of his creditors any statement of his assets and liabilities which shows that lie is insolvent, or presents or causes to be presented to any such meeting a written admission of his inability to pay his debts;

The next paragraph deals with the removal of his property so that it is not available for the settlement of his debts. Then there is the Bulk Sales Act provision, that is, if he makes a bulk sale of his property. The next reads:
If he gives notice to any of his creditors that he has suspended or that he is about to suspend payment of his debts;
My attention has been directed to that since this discussion began. The next reads:
If he ceases to meet his liabilities generally as they become due.

That was the original statute. As I said this afternoon, insolvency results from a man's inability to pay his debts as they become due, but in a country such as this, where the difficulties of making a living are so great under distress circumstances and where crops and climatic conditions have so much to do with a man's ability to meet his obligations, it was thought desirable to add the word ""general"", so that a single specific instance of inability to pay as the obligation matures should not then in itself constitute an act of bankruptcy. Those are at least the acts which if committed by a debtor are acts of bankruptcy under our statute. As the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) said

The bill contemplates a compromise being effected and an adjustment being made for the purpose of enabling a man who is in insolvent circumstances to secure from his creditors an extension of time under an agreement which would be agreed to by all his creditors, this being purely a matter between his creditors and himself. Upon failing to reach an agreement, a court of review is set up. This is an informal court consisting of a judge and representatives of the creditors and the debtor. 1038551,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.165,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,We gave some thought

to that and the reason the word ""generally"" is not inserted is this: this act is an act of the farmer under clause 6 and he will found jurisdiction to attempt a composition if he is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due. The word ""generally"" need not have any application. If he finds he is unable to meet a liability maturing to-day, he may say to-morrow: I am not able to meet this liability and I know others are coming; I must ask my creditors to make a composition. Under paragraph (j) of section 3 of the Bankruptcy Act, if he is unable to meet his liabilities as they generally become due, that constitutes an act of bankruptcy. But Part I has no reference to the farmer who is affected only by part II which deals with assignments. If, however, it is found that the insertion of that word makes the clause any better I shall not for a single moment oppose its being added. This section is for the farmer; it is permissive; it is to enable him, if he is unable to meet his debts as they become due, to have a scheme drawn up for the composition of his liabilities. The absence of the word ""generally"" is in the interest of the farmer and not against him.

The Bankruptcy Act does not apply in part I to farmers; part II, dealing with assignments, applies to farmers but neither consideration need have any weight with us at the moment. We are indicating the condition under which the farmer may apply to use this legislation; that is all. All he has to do is to be in a position where he is unable to meet his liabilities either before or after an assignment has been made. If he has made an assignment he is not able to meet his debts as they mature. If a petition is filed against him he is in the same position. He does not come under part I of the Bankruptcy Act. Therefore, so far as we are concerned there is only one question to ask: Is he unable to meet his liabilities as they become due? If so, he may use the provisions of this measure. Have I made myself clear to my hon. friend? I am afraid I have not.

1038598,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.212,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,The positions of a secured creditor and of an unsecured creditor are not the same. That is number one. The position of a secured creditor is defined by section 8 and in part by section 12. I repeat, the scheme of this bill is that one who is unable to pay his debts has a right conferred upon him, which in all probability is a right that he possesses as a citizen of this country, to approach his creditors for the purpose of endeavouring to arrive at a compromise of his liabilities and an extension of the time within which to meet his obligations. If his creditors are obdurate, he then has a right to present his claim to a board of review, and a plan or scheme is formulated looking towards the settlement of his obligation in accordance with that plan. If there are secured creditors either in the first instance or in the second, the security is to be valued, and when it reaches the court of review it will be observed from subsection 8 of section 12 that the primary factor in determining whether the scheme shall be adversely or favourably dealt with is the present and prospective capability of the debtor to perform the obligations prescribed and the productive value of the farm. That, I think it will be admitted, is a sound basis on which to approach a problem of that kind in a country where climatic conditions play so large a part in determining the ability of a farmer to meet his debts.

Then, as has been- pointed out, there is another clause, subsection 6 of section 12, providing that if the creditors or the debtor decline to approve the proposal so formulated, the board may nevertheless confirm the proposal, although it may not be acceptable to both the creditors and the debtor. Despite the fact that the plan has not been agreed upon between the debtor and the creditors, it may be approved by the board. That is, the proposal is confirmed either in the form in which it was formulated or as amended by the board itself, in which case it shall be approved by the court and shall be binding upon all the creditors and the debtor as in the case of a proposal duly accepted by the creditors and approved by the court. That is
a jurisdiction conferred upon the board in terms as broad possibly as we should go even in the light of the decision of the supreme court last Thursday.

1038618,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.232,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,Answering the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), when I met the representatives of the farm loan associations they made it perfectly clear that

what they feared was that the lands upon which they held mortgages would be abandoned by those who found it difficult to continue. It was not that they were endeavouring to find some way to secure their pound of flesh; on the contrary they were willing to consider any proposal which could be formulated in law and which would not have the effect of confiscation, which they greatly feared as a precedent, but would enable them to make such concessions as would ensure the property being valued, shall I say, at what it would be valued if they foreclosed. I will put this to the committee. A property is mortgaged for $1,000 and foreclosure proceedings are pending. Under the law of most provinces it becomes essential to put in an upset bid when a property is being sold under foreclosure proceedings. The appraiser says the property is worth $500 and it follows that unless a bid for more than $500 is received, the property falls back to the mortgagee. This contemplates something of that general spirit being carried into the legislation. When the plan is formulated, there will be a valuation by the security holder of his security. I say quite frankly to this committee that I think it will find that in most cases they will place a very low estimate upon their securities, where it is at all possible to secure something instead of nothing and to secure a continuance upon the property which otherwise would be abandoned to them. I think I can say that with some degree of frankness, because they seemed to be most desirous that that end should be attained. Under those circumstances wrhat we have endeavoured to do is to give effect to that general principle. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) says: Suppose they valued the security at $500. Well, if that represents the then value of it on foreclosure, for instance, it would be a fair valuation. What will have happened is that the loan company or the secured creditor has lost $1,200 or $1,500 as the case may be. That is not confiscation; that is what has been lost by reason of the decrease in value, the difference between its value and the value put upon it.

1038638,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.252,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,The hon. gentleman, I think, realizes as well as any member of this house does that what we are endeavouring to do is not to impinge upon the exclusive power of the provincial legislatures in dealing with property and civil rights and that, for instance, with respect to a real estate mortgage

properly registered we have no jurisdiction to make an order that the registration shall disappear. But we conceive it to be possible, under the authority of the decision of Thursday last, to declare that a tribunal set up by this parliament has power under bankruptcy to declare that for the purposes of ranking against the estate, his security shall be valued at a fixed sum and that beyond that he shall not share in the distribution of the estate. The hon. gentleman referred to the provisions as to secured creditors under the Bankruptcy Act, which provide that if he realizes his security he may prove for the balance due to him. That is, he can foreclose the mortgage, realizing 81,500, when his mortgage was $2,500, and rank against the estate for the other $1,000. That cannot happen here. Secondly, if the

If he wanted to get the benefit of the whole of his security, plus his share of what he did not have security upon, what he did was to surrender the security to the trustee, the trustee realizing upon it, and then he filed a claim for the whole of his debt with interest, and took usually the major part of the estate. We are endeavouring not to raise that issue between property and civil rights and contract with respect to security, which the province has authorized the creation of within its laws, which is registered under the authority of its jurisdiction, and at the same time maintain what we conceive to be our powers with respect to bankruptcy, dealing with it in that way. To the extent to which these clauses have application, we have not repealed them; but I have given the committee the reason why we have avoided any endeavour to precipitate a conflict between the legislature on the one hand and parliament on the other, one dealing exclusively with property and civil rights in contracts and the other dealing exclusively with bankruptcy and interest.

1038649,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.263,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,All of the provinces are more interested in our being able to sustain this legislation than otherwise. All of the provinces with which we have been in communication are anxious that should be done because they concede the difficulty of their tying on to a debt adjustment or problems that affect, shall I say, bankruptcy as it has been construed by the courts and interest, both falling within the exclusive jurisdiction of the dominion. We believe if we undertook narrowly to analyze the problem and state it in a statute we would run the risk of the statute being invalid for infringing upon the rights of the provinces. I think I can say this to the committee generally, some of whom only are lawyers, that if the swing of judicial opinion as indicated by the judgments of the privy council during the first twenty-five years of the twentieth century were to prevail, the rights of the provinces against the dominion would certainly prevail, but if, on the other hand, the swing that is indicated by more recent decisions in favour of federal powers were to prevail perhaps the federal powers would be sustained. Lord Watson was the great exponent of what one might call provincial rights in interpretation of the statutes, and Lord Haldane followed Lord Watson whom he regarded as the greatest jurist of his time. I think the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth will agree with me it would be very unsound to narrow the problem as between property and civil rights on the one hand and bankruptcy and interest on the other if we are to. run the risk of inviting

a conflict at once upon that issue. I shall deal with clause 12 when we come to it. If it is desired that clause 8 should stand until we deal with clause 12, all well and good, but I think it will be found we have gone as far as we can to assert our jurisdiction without in any respect encroaching unduly upon the jurisdiction of the provinces, because I am bearing in mind what I fancy the hon. gentleman will remind me of, that if there is a conflict under certain circumstances our legislation would prevail. 1038679,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.293,1934-06-11,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,"Mr. Chairman, on this section I should like to make a familiar request of the Prime Minister. The section reads:

The Minister of Finance shall he charged with the administration of this act, and the expenses necessary for such administration shall be payable out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.

I should like to move, unless the Prime Minister would care to do so himself, that the words ""any unappropriated moneys in the ' consolidated revenue fund"" in lines 40 and 41 be struck out and the following substituted therefor ""moneys appropriated by parliament."" I think the Prime Minister will agree that we have gone pretty far in the adoption of a new practice with respect to the control of public moneys, by asserting in these acts that moneys shall be taken out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund. It is really desirable to have the Commons control expenditure; not only that, but to have an annual report to parliament together
Farmers'-Creditors' Act

with annual appropriations, so that the total expenditure of the country will come before the house each session. If that is not done there is no way of keeping track of the total expenditure. It is also desirable in measures of this kind, which are largely experimental, to have a report to parliament of what in other respects may be done under the measures, in order to make perfectly sure that all phases of the legislation will be discussed each session.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038680,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.294,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,Well, I do hope the right hon. gentleman will not press that view. When he, in my place, had to consider the Old Age Pensions Act, in section 7 he provided that the whole sum disbursed by this dominion for old age pensions, amounting now to millions of dollars per annum, should be paid out of the unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund. Why did lie do that? He did so for the reason that it was almost impossible to arrive at any accurate estimate of the amount required; therefore he enacted in that statute the provision to which I have referred. I just thought I would send for the statute, though the words are perhaps within the memory of the bon. gentleman:

All sums payable to any province in pursuance of any agreement made under this act 6hall be payable from time to time on the certificate of the Minister of Finance out of any moneys belonging to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada not otherwise appropriated.

That was in 1927. At that time the right hon. gentleman had to assume responsibility for enacting something that would be workable, and he knew as I knew that to place in the estimates an amount which would be the result of conjecture and guess work probably would not be desirable. Hence this statute. It might be that in the second or third year, if it becomes necessary to utilize this measure for a period of years, that might be done, but obviously in the first year every argument that induced the right hon. gentleman to make that legislation effective with respect to old age pensions, involving millions of dollars, I submit is a powerful argument in favour of this section being enacted, not to authorize the payment of large sums but to provide for the expenses necessary in the administration of the measure. I trust that under those circumstances the right hon. gentleman will agree that what he found essential to make his statute practicable I find equally essential in the measure before us.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038681,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.295,1934-06-11,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,I will agree
that the Prime Minister is quite right in directing attention to what was done when

the old age pensions measure was passed, but the fact that he does direct attention to it, and that he has done so several times this session, only emphasizes what I am now attempting to assert, namely the danger that once we adopt a course that may be a departure and which is intended for one single purpose and as an exception, in the course of time it may become a regular method of procedure. I am afraid that is the direction in which we are heading at the moment. We have adopted the practice now, with respect to nearly all relief measures, of doing away with the control of the house over annual appropriations. In the marketing legislation as brought in there was the same intention expressed in the statute; afterwards it very properly was changed. If I am not mistaken there was something similar in the excise measure.

1038682,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.296,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,No, that is a case of the minister and the governor in council.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038683,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.297,1934-06-11,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Leader of the Official Opposition,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,It is all a matter of the control of expenditure. I would much rather see the Prime Minister amend the Old Age Pensions Act in the direction of requiring an annual appropriation for that purpose than to see him citing that act as a precedent in introducing other measures and thereby following what I believe to be a wrong course, even if I may have been partly responsible for acquiescing in it myself. I do think there is a tremendous danger especially in these times when we are spending very large sums of money, of the public losing sight altogether of what annually these various experiments in social, industrial and economic legislation are costing the country. It is an important aspect of all legislation, the most important in some respects. I think it should be easy to form some estimate of the amount required, and if the estimate is not sufficient the Prime Minister knows that he is at liberty to introduce supplementary estimates when the time comes. That would ensure the house getting an idea at least of what this class of legislation and this particular measure is costing the country, and it would also ensure the matter coming up for discussion each year. I would like the Prime Minister to move an amendment himself, but if he does not I shall feel obliged to ask the committee to consider an amendment.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038684,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.298,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,The right hon. gentleman is in error when he suggests that we are making an exception to the general rule. It has been the rule-I took the trouble to look through a number of the statutes the other day; when the determination of the
Farmers'-Creditors' Act

amount to be utilized is almost impossible and involves a rough guess, it is better to charge it up against the fund directly and positively than to cumber up the estimates with a statement of something of which when the minister is asked for particulars he can only say: I cannot tell you, but I guess it will be so much; it may be that much; it may be less or it may be more. I will admit that after an act has been running for a number of years one should be able to fix the amount approximately, but I do submit after looking through the statutes not only of this parliament but of other countries as well, that provisions for unappropriated moneys in the consolidated fund to be made available are usual and customary provisions.

It must also be remembered that there is a limitation; the revenue must be there. The expenditure cannot transcend the revenue, for then there is no unappropriated balance in the fund. That is perfectly obvious. Secondly, the sums of money that we pay under statutory authority are detailed every year in the auditor general's report, and their ultimate destination is indicated. I suggest to the right hon. gentleman, therefore, that we are not asking too much when we suggest that this should be left as it is, at least until we we see what is involved, and then if in the light of the experience and the knowledge obtained in the operation of the act for a year one is able to predicate even with any degree of certainty the amount that will be required, it should be introduced in the estimates. I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman as to the broad general principle of the control of the Commons House of Parliament over the expenditures of the country. That is true. But the fact that during all these years, nearly seventy years since confederation, we have found it necessary to make these appropriations in this way is an indication that there are exceptions to well defined rules which in themselves constitute the reason and the authority for the rule, and here, if ever, is a case in which neither the Minister of Finance nor myself can do anything more than guess at the sum that may be required.

Let me just put it this way. If there are extraordinarily good crops and a return by reason of bountiful rains to a measure of prosperity on the farms of Ontario, where there has been a shortage of certain crops, and in other provinces the same, I could not tell whether it would be necessary to spend five or five hundred dollars in any one province. It would be a plain guess in the dark. But when the expenditures have been made,
I repeat, and with the knowledge of another year, I shall be perfectly content, sitting on either side of the house, to agree that an appropriation might well appear in the estimates.

1038686,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.300,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,In the discussions that have taken place, knowing as I do the economic conditions that prevail throughout the country, I did not think it would cost very much for salaries in connection with the administration of the act. The official receiver, so called, I had thought would not be a highly [DOT] expensive official, and the first review that would have to be made would be the extent to which it would be necessary to utilize the provisions of this act in the several provinces; then the length of time that it might be necessary for the officials to act during a year. For instance, I know that in the winter time it is exceedingly difficult for them to view the properties or to have inspections made that would enable them to deal authoritatively with them, and that is true of almost every part of Canada. I confess that I may have underestimated what it might cost, but I thought that men could be secured for part time effort in that direction for perhaps $150 per month in some of these matters, and in some cases retired men who have had experience in valuation and matters of that sort.

I thought it would not be a very expensive process. In the case of old age pensions, for instance, we were able to estimate from the census the number of people who would receive a pension, and in one province in particular the sum has been known for years, and was stated as one of the difficulties to be met in dealing with old age pensions. I am divulging no secret when I say that in this case the question of expense is all important, and we discussed the question how we might limit it to the smallest possible amount consistent with some measure of efficiency. I could not to-night indicate to the right hon. gentleman any sum at all that would be adequate for the purpose any more than it would be possible to indicate what sum might be required for a service that had never been given, and this is a new service in a sense.
Farmers'-Creditors' Act

We were given some information as to the sums expended under the debt adjustment acts in the three western provinces, and I think they have something similar in British Columbia, although I believe the act is not known there by that name. I am not sure if that is a correct statement of the situation or not. In Ontario there was also an endeavour to make some adjustments in that way. The salaries paid in the western provinces were small. I mentioned $150 a month for part time work. The hon. member who has just come in (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) knows that the debt adjustment officer in Alberta received moderately small compensation, and the first one, Mr. Fream, was a particularly good man. In a province as large as Saskatchewan I think they have two. In Manitoba I think the official gets small compensation. If I could enlighten the right hon. gentleman I would do so, but I am sorry I cannot do it.

Mr. Chairman, what I think the right hon. gentleman will realize at once is sound, namely that that depends upon the extent to which farmers make applications and proposals. The hon. gentlemen who sit beside the right hon. leader, one from Alberta and the other from Manitoba, will tell you that that is something which depends as much upon psychological reasons as upon physical reasons. Anyone who has lived in the west for thirty years and over as I have knows that they are never discouraged or overwhelmed. If you tell them that there are prospects that the grasshoppers are all dead or dying, that the rains are bountiful, and that there is no chance of frost, the chances are that they will say: Well, we are not going to try to compromise; if possible we want to pay one hundred cents on the dollar. ,,,An hon. MEMBER:,
1038713,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.9.327,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,FARMERS'-CREDITORS' ACT,,,I am speaking of corporate official receivers. In the mercantile community you have a different set of considerations. As a matter of fact I think they have much of the legislation now in Saskatchewan to enable them to avail themselves of it; they certainly have in Ontario. But the truth, I suppose, is that there is difficulty in obtaining money for farm loans in Saskatchewan under any circumstances at the present time. The province of Saskatchewan created its own loan organization many years ago; in fact one who was at one time minister of finance here had the direction of the board. The present condition of the loans, as far as my memory goes, is that the board is not active; therefore they are not in a position to find new capital. But I believe they have taken collateral security to ensure the province against loss as far as possible. If my memory serves me, the losses have been very substantial.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038750,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.28,1934-06-11,2c4fde50-eb86-4288-a3d6-0ecb43786cf0,ca.m.6767,Mr. LUCAS:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,Will the Prime Minister say by what method Ontario raises money for its farm loans? I understand loans were made at five and a half per cent and the rate has been recently reduced to five per cent. That is a lower rate than we have been paying under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. I am wondering by what method they were able to get money cheaper than the dominion.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,William Thomas Lucas,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2c4fde50-eb86-4288-a3d6-0ecb43786cf0&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038751,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.29,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,They have not been able to get money cheaper than the dominion. What they have done is hold themselves out as the recipient and custodian of the savings of the people, for which they paid a rate of interest in excess of that paid by the chartered banks. The moneys thus received were loaned on mortgages and the rate was slightly in excess of that paid for the deposits. In Manitoba the same plan was tried and there were 40,000 depositors. Their money had been lent on mortgages and when the people wanted their money the savings department had the promises to pay of the province of Manitoba which had taken the money for their farm loan board and loaned it to the farmers. Inasmuch as there is a
Farm Loan Act

vast difference between bank notes and cash on the one hand and farm mortgages on the other in the safety deposit boxes, they found themselves compelled to secure a loan for the purpose of enabling them to meet their obligations. There is a great difference of opinion in the minds of those who are charged with financial responsibility as to whether or not the scheme which for years has been in practice in Ontario is of the soundest. But that is how it is done; my business is to answer the question,' and that is the answer.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038752,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.30,1934-06-11,2c4fde50-eb86-4288-a3d6-0ecb43786cf0,ca.m.6767,Mr. LUCAS:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,I notice in this bill that the dominion is to guarantee the bonds that are to be sold. I was wondering how they are going to accept that responsibility, and whether the post office saving department might not be a great source of cheap money to supply these loans.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,William Thomas Lucas,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2c4fde50-eb86-4288-a3d6-0ecb43786cf0&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038753,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.31,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,The hon. gentleman is aware that under the provisions of the statute generally the price at which money is obtained by the board is the determining factor as to the price paid by the borrower. The borrower pays one and one-half per cent more than the cost of the money to the board, one per cent being for administration and one-half of one per cent for the incidentals in connection with the maintenance of the business. If Canada borrows at four per cent it can lend at five and a half; if at three and a half per cent, it can lend at five. That is the difference between the two plans to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

On the question of obtaining money through the post office savings department I can only point out that it has not been thus far a savings depository favoured by the people of the country. The entire sum now on deposit in the post office savings bank, if my memory serves me-and I speak wholly from memory -is between $20,000,000 and $25,000,000. It has not increased in recent years, but broadly and generally has diminished, because it has not been a favoured institution for the lodging of the savings of the people. I am told the amount on deposit at the present time is $28,000,000.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038754,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.32,1934-06-11,717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a,ca.m.5259,Mr. COOTE:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,The ability of the farmer to repay his loans is determined in large part by the rate of interest which he must pay, and it seems to me that the rate of interest might very well be reduced by the farm loan board now. I believe the dominion government can borrow money at the present time at less than four per cent. If that is true would it not be possible for the farm loan board to reduce the interest rate?

,United Farmers of Alberta,,George Gibson Coote,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038755,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.33,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,If the hon. gentleman

had followed what I said a moment ago he would have realized that there is an addition of one and a half per cent as the statute now stands, one per cent for administration charges and one-half of one per cent in connection with the charges of the transaction.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038756,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.34,1934-06-11,717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a,ca.m.5259,Mr. COOTE:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,Is that in the statute or is
it the policy of the board?

,United Farmers of Alberta,,George Gibson Coote,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038757,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.35,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,That is in the statute

itself. The result is that borrowings at four per cent have to be lent at five and a half per cent, and borrowings at three and a half per cent would be lent at five per cent. That differentiates the organization from the farm loan board of Ontario, which lends the moneys it collects from the savings deposited in the savings offices, upon which at one time they paid four per cent interest.

1038759,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.37,1934-06-11,717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a,ca.m.5259,Mr. COOTE:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,"If it is intended or hoped that the farm loan board will be able to make loans to people who would like to pay off mortgages now bearing interest at eight per cent there will be a great many cases in which the existing loan is on a piece of land separate from the quarter section on which the buildings of the farmer are located. In the past it has been a practice of the board-I do not know that it is a regulation-to refuse to give loans to farmers unless they put the quarter section on which their buildings were located in with the piece of property to be mortgaged to the board. This makes it very unfortunate in many cases. It simply means that a farmer cannot get a mortgage unless he mortgages his home. The primary purpose of this legislation is to save the farmers' homes for the farmers even though they might have to let go other pieces of land. Under this section I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the farm loan board are compelled in any way to follow that rule. It seems to me it is just a rule they have laid down themselves. Sometimes it is attended with unfortunate results, in that the farmer is perhaps compelled to mortgage his home, which otherwise he would not want to do.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,George Gibson Coote,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038760,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.38,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,The hon. gentleman is

perhaps fully aware that the policy has been adopted by the board and not by the government. The board has endeavoured to function as free from governmental interference as possible, and in the light of the experience of the past that is the conclusion at which they
Farm Loan Act

arrived in promulgating their regulations. They decided that they were not warranted in treating the moneys entrusted to them for lending on any basis that would not, so far as that might be done, ensure their repayment, and they have taken securities on that basis. Frankly that is the policy as indicated by the board when it came into being.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038761,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.39,1934-06-11,717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a,ca.m.5259,Mr. COOTE:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,The board was empowered to lend money to enable the farmer to purchase lands, and certainly in some cases it is poor policy on the part of the board to insist that the farmer place his home under mortgage before he can borrow anything. It may be that they would then be compelled to lend a smaller percentage of the appraised value of the land, but so far as I know they have followed that rule. I think in some cases it is a poor rule for the board to fallow, and perhaps this is the only opportunity I will have of raising that question while the representative of the board is here with the Prime Minister.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,George Gibson Coote,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038762,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.40,1934-06-11,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,There is nothing that can be added, except that as a matter of policy that is the rule that has been adopted, and that is all that can be said about it. It might be said, however, that it has been a universal rule in making loans that the property on which the house is built should be included in the mortgage. I know of no case in which that is not the rule of all the companies in the country, in order that there might be a direct incentive on the part of the man who borrowed the .money not to abandon the piece of property and let it go but rather, feeling that his home was involved, that he should make an extra effort to pay the loan. Frankly I must say that the policy of the board as far as I could ascertain.-and I came as a stranger and inquirer-has been exactly what it would be if it were a loan company, and it has been conducted as such. I think that is a fair way to put it.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1038763,ca.proc.d.1934-06-11.10.1.41,1934-06-11,717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a,ca.m.5259,Mr. COOTE:,,CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT,PROVISION TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS,,I think it has been conducted more conservatively than most loan companies. I could' find thousands of quarter sections without farm buildings on which loans have been made by loan companies, but I do not find the same practice being followed by the board. I think the time has come when we might consider changing our laws with regard to the interest rates on farm mortgages, and provide that a man's house need not necessarily go with the mortgage. The position of the ordinary business man who mortgages his business is different from that of the farmer. The

business man does not have to mortgage his home; if he goes into bankruptcy he does not lose his home. The farmer is in a different category; if he wants to get an advance under mortgage he must put in his home. If he wants to take advantage of bankruptcy proceedings to get rid of debts he must throw in his home and be forced into the street. Really I think if the government is depending upon the operation of this farm loan board to bring about a reduction in the rate of interest on farm mortgages their practice in that regard ought to be changed, to that degree at least.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,George Gibson Coote,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=717ab1d6-e8dc-480c-aba9-4552f242369a&Language=E&Section=ALL
